entries.title: Conclusion

exact_difference.detail: Black Hat Rust ch.14 conclusion: mostly career and ethics material (bug bounty platforms, selling a scanner as SaaS, selling a RAT, leaked Hacking Team / Vault7 repos, how attackers get caught, contact details). Its one engineering claim is section 14.1.1: 'I don't like lifetime annotations... Do you and your coworkers a favor: avoid lifetime annotations. Instead, whenever it's possible, prefer to move data, or when it's not possible, use smart pointers such as Rc and Arc for long-lived references,' presented as a goal the whole book was written to prove.

entries.remaining_uncertainty: dispositioned at chapter granularity: the reason describes the chapter this heading belongs to, not the heading in isolation. Contradicts own-lifetime-elision, which documents when explicit lifetimes ARE required (structs holding references, multiple ambiguous inputs); contradicts own-arc-shared, which scopes Arc to shared ownership crossing thread boundaries rather than as a general substitute for borrows; and contradicts own-borrow-over-clone. The chapter's parallel advice on macros ('think twice before writing a macro') is instead ALIGNED with macro-prefer-functions, so this is not a wholesale deviation chapter. It also does not establish whether the book's earlier chapters actually follow the no-lifetimes rule in their code.

entries.title: What is Web Assembly?

entries.title: Intro to Web Assembly

exact_difference.detail: Conceptual introduction to WebAssembly: what Wasm is, its four value types, linear memory model, and stack-machine execution.

entries.remaining_uncertainty: Explanatory background about the Wasm platform, not a Rust engineering-practice contract.

entries.title: Rust in the browser

exact_difference.detail: Explains WebAssembly's stack machine execution model, LLVM/Wasm targets and target triples, and the steps to create a minimal wasm32-unknown-unknown cdylib.

entries.remaining_uncertainty: Does not state any engineering-contract practice the rule library covers.

entries.title: The Smallest Wasm Library

exact_difference.detail: Walks through creating an empty wasm cdylib, target triples/rustup, and shrinking the 1.4M binary to 71 bytes with wasm-strip and wasm-opt.

entries.remaining_uncertainty: Binary-size stripping via external tools has no clean contract in the library (which favors retaining symbols); no practice mapped.

entries.title: Working with primatives

exact_difference.detail: WASM tutorial: builds a cdylib 'add' function with #[no_mangle] extern "C", shrinks the .wasm with wasm-strip/wasm-opt, and hosts it from an HTML/JS page via instantiateStreaming.

entries.remaining_uncertainty: Explains no_mangle/extern C mechanics for a worked WASM example rather than stating a general library-design contract.

entries.title: Working with complex types

exact_difference.detail: the unit constructs a host-side typed array over the module's linear memory and frees what it allocated in a finally block, and its surrounding pages hand-marshal a String across the boundary by having the host read raw pointer/length words out of the struct's private layout; ffi-wasm-memory-view adds that any call which can grow memory invalidates that view, and ffi-wasm-wire-abi adds that the (ptr, len) pair must be an explicit, documented wire contract rather than a read of #[repr(Rust)]'s undocumented layout

entries.remaining_uncertainty: the wire-ABI assertion runs on a 64-bit host, not a real wasm32 target, so ptr/len are u64 there instead of the u32 a real WASM export would use; the marshalling shape is the same

entries.title: The Real Way to Write Wasm

exact_difference.detail: Step-by-step tutorial packaging a greet() function with wasm-bindgen/wasm-pack into an NPM module (hello-bindgen) and calling it from a webpack JS app.

entries.remaining_uncertainty: Teaches the wasm-bindgen toolchain mechanics for one worked example; no reusable library contract asserted.
